html:
Dutch New Guinea was the western half of the island of New Guinea, held by the Netherlands as part of the Dutch East Indies and, after 1949, as a separate colony until 1962. The map labels it "Dutch Guinea" and shows it in 1945; the Dutch Gold Coast in Africa went by the same name.

The Dutch claimed the area from 1828, mainly to keep other powers out, but for most of the 1800s they had almost no presence there. Government posts were only set up at places such as Manokwari and Fakfak in 1898. The interior, home to many Papuan peoples, was hardly known.

In 1942 Japan occupied much of the coast in the Second World War. Allied forces landed at Hollandia, now Jayapura, in April 1944. When Indonesia won independence in 1949, the Netherlands kept western New Guinea and prepared it for self-rule. Under pressure, it handed the territory over in 1962, through a short United Nations administration, to Indonesia in 1963. A disputed vote in 1969, the Act of Free Choice, confirmed Indonesian rule, and a Papuan independence movement has continued since. The island's eastern half is Papua New Guinea.
